ind:nhwa-4-03:
Indicator. 4-03 Share of women in leadership role

NHWA indicator 4-03: Share of women in leadership role. Share of women in senior management positions in the Ministry of Health

Numerator Denominator Disaggregation
Number of women in leadership roles in the Ministry of Health, defined in headcounts Total number of men and women in leadership roles in the Ministry of Health, defined in headcounts not printed in the NHWA handbook; for the working group

Definition: Share of women, expressed as a percentage, of women in senior management positions in the Ministry of Health. To monitor and report on this indicator, it is advised to count all individuals at director-level or equivalent positions within the Ministry of Health. Using the organigram of the Ministry of Health, focusing on the senior positions, should be sufficient to estimate this indicator. Alternative approaches could be based on the count of men and women in delegations participating to the annual World Health Assemblies.

Potential data sources: Ministry of Health organigram or official documents.

Reporting: Every three years.

Data elements in this chapter: de:nhwa-m4-leadership-position.

Source: National health workforce accounts: a handbook, 2nd edition, indicator 4-03 (page 87), word for word, from the ingested L1 node in who-iris. Draft L2 indicator NHWA.4-03, for working-group review.
ind:nhwa-4-04:
Indicator. 4-04 International Health Regulations implementation capacity

NHWA indicator 4-04: International Health Regulations implementation capacity. Availability of human resources to implement International Health Regulations core capacity requirements (None/Limited/Developed/Demonstrated/ Sustainable)

Numerator Denominator Disaggregation
not printed in the NHWA handbook; for the working group not printed in the NHWA handbook; for the working group not printed in the NHWA handbook; for the working group

Definition: This indicator is based on indicator D3.2 of the Joint External Evaluation (JEE) tool, third edition (which is similar to indicator C6.1 in State Party Self-assessment Annual Reporting (SAPR) tool), and it uses the following (capability) items: No capacity (level 1) Country does not have appropriate human resources capacity in relevant sectors required to detect, assess, notify, report and respond to events according to IHR provisions Limited capacity (level 2) Appropriate human resources are available in some relevant sectors at the national level to detect, assess, notify, report and respond to events according to IHR provisions Developed capacity (level 3) Appropriate human resources are available in all relevant sectors at national and intermediate levels to detect, assess, notify, report and respond to events according to IHR provisions Demonstrated capacity (level 4) Human resources are available as required in all relevant sectors at the national, intermediate and primary public health levels to detect, assess, notify, report and respond to events according to IHR provisions Sustainable capacity (level 5) Country has documented policies or procedures for sustainable appropriate human resources in all relevant sectors to detect, assess, notify, report and respond to events according to IHR provisions, that are exercised (as applicable), reviewed, evaluated and updated on a regular basis, and country may assist other countries in planning and developing human resources for IHR implementation, to the extent possible

Potential data sources: Ministry of Health; Public health institutions.

Reporting: Every three years. Frameworks: Joint External Evaluation (JEE), State Party Self-Assessment Annual Reporting Tool (SPAR).

Source: National health workforce accounts: a handbook, 2nd edition, indicator 4-04 (page 88), word for word, from the ingested L1 node in who-iris. Draft L2 indicator NHWA.4-04, for working-group review.
ind:nhwa-4-05:
Indicator. 4-05 National capacity to monitor key metrics for health workforce planning and global monitoring frameworks

NHWA indicator 4-05: National capacity to monitor key metrics for health workforce planning and global monitoring frameworks. Capacity of national human resources for health information systems to monitor key metrics relevant for national health workforce planning and policy-making and for global monitoring frameworks

Numerator Denominator Disaggregation
not printed in the NHWA handbook; for the working group not printed in the NHWA handbook; for the working group not printed in the NHWA handbook; for the working group

Definition: This indicator is a composite of nine sub-indicators, see below. The response to these nine sub-indicators is aggregated as a score (see part II on methods) on a scale from 1 (nascent) to 5 (sustainable). Each sub-indicator is a self-assessment of one aspect of the capacity of the national human resources for health information system (HRHIS) or other mechanisms to report on key metrics that are relevant for national health workforce planning and policy-making as well as for global monitoring frameworks. To help answer some of these self-assessed sub-indicators, guiding questions are provided.

Sub-indicators:

  • 4-05.1 Ability of HIS to report on HRH data (Yes/Partial/No/Not applicable)
  • 4-05.2 Ability of HRHIS (or other mechanism) to generate information to report on health workforce metrics for International Health Regulations (IHR) (Yes/Partial/No)
  • 4-05.3 Ability of HRHIS (or other mechanism) to generate information to report on implementation of the WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel (Yes/Partial/No)
  • 4-05.4 Ability of HRHIS to generate information for reporting on outputs from education and training institutions (Yes/Partial/No)
  • 4-05.5 Ability of HRHIS to generate information to track entrants to the labour market (Yes/Partial/No)
  • 4-05.6 Ability of HRHIS to generate information to track active stock on the labour market (Yes/Partial/No)
  • 4-05.7 Ability of HRHIS to generate information to track exits from the labour market (Yes/Partial/No)
  • 4-05.8 Ability of HRHIS to generate geocoded information on the location of health facilities (Yes/Partial/No)
  • 4-05.9 Ability of HRHIS to monitor gender pay gap (Yes/Partial/No)

Potential data sources: Ministry of Health and regional ministries of health; Professional chambers; Institutions or units responsible for monitoring, or for policies on the health workforce; Ministry of Labour; National Statistical Office; National Focal Point for WHO Global Code of Practice; Ministry of Health and subnational ministries of health; Institutions collecting health workforce data.

Reporting: Annual. Frameworks: Global Strategy for Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030 (GSHRH), Working for Health programme, Global Strategic Directions for Nursing and Midwifery (SDNM), SCORE for Health Data Technical Package (SCORE).

Source: National health workforce accounts: a handbook, 2nd edition, indicator 4-05 (pages 89-90), word for word, from the ingested L1 node in who-iris. Draft L2 indicator NHWA.4-05, for working-group review.

prose:ch12-objectives:
Chapter objectives. This chapter will help readers to:

  • Apply privacy by design to health workers' personal data.
  • Identify the security controls that a registry needs.
  • Describe how access is controlled and audited so that stakeholders can trust the registry.
prose:ch12-key-messages:
Key messages

  • A registry holds personal data about health workers. Protecting those data is a legal and ethical duty.
  • Decide what is public, what is shared between institutions and what is restricted, and be open about it.
  • Security is a continuous activity, not a one-off installation.
  • Trust depends on transparency: health workers should know who uses their data and why.
prose:ch12-privacy-by-design:
• Collect the minimum data needed, use them only for stated purposes, and set retention limits.
  • Carry out a privacy impact assessment before implementation and before major changes.
  • Tiered disclosure: a public view, an institutional view and restricted data.
prose:ch12-cybersecurity:
• Risk assessment, secure hosting, encryption of stored and transmitted data, backup and recovery.
  • Incident response and notification of data breaches.
  • Alignment with national cybersecurity policies and standards.
prose:ch12-access-control:
• Role-based access for people; authenticated and authorized access for systems.
  • Self-service access for health workers to their own record.
  • Regular review of user accounts and permissions.
prose:ch12-audit-trails:
• A log of who viewed or changed which record, when and why.
  • Routine review of logs, with reports to the governance body.
  • Use of audit data to detect misuse and fraud.
prose:ch12-figures:
Suggested figures and tables

  • Figure: tiered data access model.
  • Table: main threats and the controls that address them.
  • Table: roles and permissions.
prose:ch12-tools:
Implementation tools and checklists

  • Privacy impact assessment template.
  • Security checklist.
  • Roles and permissions template.
prose:ch12-outputs:
Expected outputs for countries

  • A completed privacy impact assessment.
  • A data classification and disclosure policy.
  • A security plan.
prose:ch13-objectives:
Chapter objectives. This chapter will help readers to:

  • Define data quality for a registry and how to measure it.
  • Describe validation when data are entered and when they are compared across sources.
  • Set up routine monitoring and improvement of data quality.
prose:ch13-key-messages:
Key messages

  • A registry is only as useful as its data are complete, accurate and current.
  • Quality is best assured at source, by the institution that owns the data.
  • Routine use of the data is the strongest driver of quality.
  • Data quality needs named responsibility and regular reporting.
prose:ch13-quality-dimensions:
• Completeness, accuracy, timeliness, uniqueness, consistency and validity.
  • Coverage: the proportion of the actual workforce that is in the registry, including the private sector.
  • Targets for each dimension.
prose:ch13-validation:
• Automated rules at data entry (formats, mandatory fields, code lists).
  • Verification against primary sources, such as training institutions, the national identity system and the issuing regulator.
  • Procedures for finding and resolving duplicate records.
prose:ch13-monitoring:
• Data quality indicators and dashboards.
  • Periodic audits and reconciliation with payroll, facility staffing lists or census data.
  • Feedback to data suppliers and corrective action.
prose:ch13-figures:
Suggested figures and tables

  • Table: data quality dimensions with example indicators.
  • Figure: data quality improvement cycle.
prose:ch13-tools:
Implementation tools and checklists

  • Data quality assessment checklist.
  • Catalogue of validation rules.
  • Standard operating procedure template for resolving duplicates.
prose:ch13-outputs:
Expected outputs for countries

  • A data quality plan with indicators and targets.
  • A routine data quality report.
prose:ch14-part-purpose: Part 3. Country Implementation. This part guides countries through the practical steps of transformation, from preparing and assessing readiness to operating and improving the registry. Countries can enter at the step that matches their situation.
prose:ch14-objectives:
Chapter objectives. This chapter will help readers to:

  • Secure leadership and form the team that will lead the transformation.
  • Assess readiness and the current state of registry-related systems.
  • Engage the stakeholders on whose participation the registry depends.
prose:ch14-key-messages:
Key messages

  • Joint leadership by the health workforce and digital health units is essential.
  • A readiness assessment prevents costly surprises later.
  • Regulators and professional councils are partners and data owners, not only data suppliers.
  • Agree the vision and first-phase scope before choosing technology.
prose:ch14-leadership:
• An executive sponsor and a clear mandate.
  • A shared vision and goals linked to the national health workforce and digital health strategies.
  • The registry's place in the national digital health architecture and investment plans.
prose:ch14-teams:
• Core team: health workforce lead, digital health lead, regulator representatives, business analyst, architect, data manager and legal adviser.
  • Roles, responsibilities and time commitment.
  • When to bring in external technical support.
prose:ch14-readiness:
• Assessment areas: governance and law, data, processes, technology and infrastructure, people and skills, and financing.
  • An inventory of existing registers and systems.
  • Placement on the maturity model and identification of gaps.
prose:ch14-stakeholder-engagement:
• Stakeholder mapping, with analysis of interests and influence.
  • Engagement methods: workshops, one-to-one consultation with councils, and dialogue with health worker associations.
  • Responding to concerns about loss of control, workload and use of data.
prose:ch14-figures:
Suggested figures and tables

  • Figure: team structure.
  • Table: readiness assessment areas and sample questions.
  • Figure: stakeholder map.
prose:ch14-tools:
Implementation tools and checklists

  • Readiness assessment (annex).
  • Stakeholder mapping template.
  • Team terms of reference template.
prose:ch14-outputs:
Expected outputs for countries

  • A mandated team and a vision statement.
  • A readiness assessment report.
  • A stakeholder engagement plan.
prose:ch15-objectives:
Chapter objectives. This chapter will help readers to:

  • Document how registration, licensing and related processes work today.
  • Design improved processes that make use of digital capabilities.
  • Derive system requirements from the redesigned processes.
prose:ch15-key-messages:
Key messages

  • Digitizing a poor process produces a poor digital process. Simplify first.
  • Mapping processes with the people who do the work reveals the real bottlenecks.
  • Redesign should reduce the burden on health workers.
  • Some process changes need regulatory or policy change. Identify these early.
prose:ch15-current-state-mapping:
• Map priority processes: first registration, licence renewal, verification, transfer and exit.
  • Record the steps, people involved, documents, time taken and difficulties.
  • Identify duplication across institutions.
